question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Nisha wishes (a)/ that she knows how (b)/ to swim like her brother. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "wish", the past tense is used for an unreal or impossible present situation. So "she knows how" must be "she knew how".

◦ Corrected sentence: Nisha wishes that she knew how to swim like her brother.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Nisha wishes" is proper, with the singular verb "wishes" agreeing with "Nisha".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to swim like her brother." is proper, with "how" followed by a to-infinitive and "like" used to compare.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "knows" in part (b) is in the present tense after "wishes", where the past tense is needed.

 

NOTE

 

• I wish I knew the answer, She wishes she were taller (past tense for an unreal present); I wish I had known (past perfect for an unreal past).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Ever since the new highway (a)/ was opened, (b)/ the travel time between the two cities (c)/ reduced by half. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When the "since" clause is in the simple past, the main clause takes the present perfect, because the result continues up to now. So "reduced by half" must be "has reduced by half".

◦ Corrected sentence: Ever since the new highway was opened, the travel time between the two cities has reduced by half.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Ever since the new highway" is proper, with "ever since" introducing a clause and "the new highway" as a specific road.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "was opened," is proper, with the simple past passive in the "since" clause.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the travel time between the two cities" is proper, with "between" used for two places.

 

NOTE

 

• Since he joined, he has improved; Ever since she left, we have missed her (simple past after "since", present perfect in the main clause).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If it will rain tomorrow, (a)/ the match will (b)/ be postponed (c)/ till Friday. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a first conditional, the "if" clause takes the simple present and the main clause takes "will + base verb". "Will" is not used in the "if" clause, so "will rain" must be "rains".

◦ Corrected sentence: If it rains tomorrow, the match will be postponed till Friday.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the match will" is proper, with "will" used in the main clause of the first conditional.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "be postponed" is proper, with "will be" followed by the past participle to form the passive.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "till Friday." is proper, with "till" used before a point of time.

 

NOTE

 

• If it rains, we will stay home, If you work hard, you will succeed (simple present in the "if" clause, "will" in the main clause).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

So far this year, (a)/ the department (b)/ issued over ten thousand (c)/ trade licences. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "So far" points to a period that continues up to now, so the present perfect is used. So "issued" must be "has issued".

◦ Corrected sentence: So far this year, the department has issued over ten thousand trade licences.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "So far this year," is proper, as an introductory phrase for a period that is not yet over.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the department" is proper, as a singular subject that acts as one unit.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "trade licences." is proper, with the plural noun "licences" after "ten thousand".

 

NOTE

 

• So far, we have sold ten books, Till now, he has not replied (present perfect with "so far / till now").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The new stadium (a)/ is building (b)/ near the airport (c)/ for the Asian Games. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A stadium cannot build itself, and the action is done to it, so the passive is needed. The present continuous passive is "is / are + being + past participle". So "is building" must be "is being built".

◦ Corrected sentence: The new stadium is being built near the airport for the Asian Games.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The new stadium" is proper, with "the" used for a specific stadium.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "near the airport" is proper, with "near" showing place.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "for the Asian Games." is proper, with "for" showing the purpose.

 

NOTE

 

• The bridge is being built, The road was being repaired (passive continuous), and not The bridge is building.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The suspect was (a)/ questioned for hours (b)/ and later (c)/ was took to the lock-up. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passive is formed with "be + past participle (V3)". "Took" is the past form, and the past participle of "take" is "taken". So "was took" must be "was taken".

◦ Corrected sentence: The suspect was questioned for hours and later was taken to the lock-up.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The suspect was" is proper, with the singular "was" agreeing with "The suspect".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "questioned for hours" is proper, with the past participle after "was" and "for" used with a period of time.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and later" is proper, with "and" joining the two passive verbs and "later" as an adverb.

 

NOTE

 

• take → took → taken; was taken, was given, was written (the passive takes V3), and not was took, was gave, was wrote.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

It is the second time (a)/ this week that the train (b)/ arrived late (c)/ at the terminal. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "It is the first / second / third time that", the present perfect is used. So "arrived late" must be "has arrived late".

◦ Corrected sentence: It is the second time this week that the train has arrived late at the terminal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "It is the second time" is proper, with the ordinal number preceded by "the".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "this week that the train" is proper, with "that" introducing the clause and "the train" as a specific train.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "at the terminal." is proper, with "at" used for a point of arrival.

 

NOTE

 

• It is the first time I have seen a lion (present perfect); It was the first time I had seen a lion (past perfect when "It was").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The workshop began (a)/ next Monday, so we will (b)/ register before Friday. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Next Monday" and "we will register" show a future time, and the simple past cannot be used for a future event. A future event takes "will + base verb", so "began" must be "will begin".

◦ Corrected sentence: The workshop will begin next Monday, so we will register before Friday.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "next Monday, so we will" is proper, because "next Monday" takes no preposition and "so" joins the two clauses.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "register before Friday." is proper, with "before" showing the time limit.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "began" in part (a) is a simple past used with the future time "next Monday".

 

NOTE

 

• The workshop will begin next Monday, The exam will start tomorrow (future time, future form), and not The workshop began next Monday.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Yesterday, the lift was out of order, (a)/ so the old woman has to (b)/ climb up to the fifth floor. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Yesterday" and "was" show that the events are in the past, so the second clause must also be in the past. So "has to" must be "had to".

◦ Corrected sentence: Yesterday, the lift was out of order, so the old woman had to climb up to the fifth floor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Yesterday, the lift was out of order," is proper, with the simple past "was" and "out of order" meaning "not working".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "climb up to the fifth floor." is proper, with "the" used before the ordinal number "fifth".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "has to" in part (b) is in the present tense, while the sentence is about yesterday.

 

NOTE

 

• Yesterday, she was ill, so she had to stay at home (keep both clauses in the past).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

After the referee had blown the whistle, (a)/ the players walked off (b)/ the field. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. Of two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect ("had blown") and the later one takes the simple past ("walked off").

◦ Sentence as given: After the referee had blown the whistle, the players walked off the field.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "After the referee had blown the whistle," is proper, with the past perfect for the earlier action.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the players walked off" is proper, with the simple past for the later action.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the field." is proper, because "walked off" needs no extra preposition before "the field".

 

NOTE

 

• After the bell had rung, the students left; The train had left before we reached (past perfect for the earlier action).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The night guard heard a loud noise, (a)/ grabbed his torch and (b)/ rush to the gate. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Verbs joined by "and" or a comma in a series of past actions must be in the same tense. "Heard" and "grabbed" are in the simple past, so "rush" must be "rushed".

◦ Corrected sentence: The night guard heard a loud noise, grabbed his torch and rushed to the gate.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The night guard heard a loud noise," is proper, with the simple past "heard".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "grabbed his torch and" is proper, with the simple past "grabbed" and "his" showing possession.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "rush" in part (c) is in the present form, while "heard" and "grabbed" are in the simple past.

 

NOTE

 

• He opened the door, looked out and shouted (all verbs in the same tense), and not He opened the door, looked out and shout.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

She has been knowing (a)/ the family (b)/ for many years. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Stative verbs (know, like, love, believe, understand) are not used in the continuous tense, even with "for" or "since". So "has been knowing" must be "has known".

◦ Corrected sentence: She has known the family for many years.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the family" is proper, with "the" used for a specific family.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "for many years." is proper, with "for" used before a period of time.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "has been knowing" in part (a) is a continuous form of the stative verb "know".

 

NOTE

 

• I have known him for years, She has loved music since childhood (present perfect), and not I have been knowing, She has been loving.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Why did the committee (a)/ rejected (b)/ his application? (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After the auxiliary "did", the base form of the verb is used, because "did" already carries the past tense. So "rejected" must be "reject".

◦ Corrected sentence: Why did the committee reject his application?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Why did the committee" is proper, with "did" as the auxiliary in a question and "the committee" as a singular subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "his application?" is proper, with the possessive "his" before the noun.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "rejected" in part (b) is a past form after "did".

 

NOTE

 

• Why did he leave?, When did she arrive? (did + base verb), and not Why did he left?, When did she arrived?.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Ravi has not prepared at all for tomorrow's test, so he ___ badly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. is going to fail.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Is / am / are going to + base verb" is used for a prediction based on present evidence. Ravi has not prepared, and this is the evidence that he will fail tomorrow, so the correct answer is "is going to fail".

◦ Complete sentence: Ravi has not prepared at all for tomorrow's test, so he is going to fail badly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "fails" — this is a simple present, which shows a habit or a fact, and it does not predict a result on "tomorrow".

 

• Option 2: "is failing" — this is a present continuous, which shows a failure happening now, but the test has not yet taken place.

 

• Option 4: "has failed" — this is a present perfect, which shows a completed failure, but the test is tomorrow.

 

NOTE

 

• Look at those clouds, it is going to rain; He has not studied, so he is going to fail (going to for a prediction from present evidence).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The receptionist informed us that the doctor is examining another patient at that moment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. was examining.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In reported speech, when the reporting verb ("informed") is in the past tense, the present continuous of the original statement changes to the past continuous. "At that moment" also points to an action in progress. So "is examining" must be "was examining".

◦ Corrected sentence: The receptionist informed us that the doctor was examining another patient at that moment.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "had examined" — this is a past perfect, which shows a completed action, but "at that moment" shows an action in progress.

 

• Option 2: "has examined" — this is a present perfect, and it does not change to the past after the past-tense verb "informed".

 

• Option 3: "examines" — this is a simple present, and it neither changes to the past nor shows an action in progress.

 

NOTE

 

• She said, "I am reading" → She said that she was reading (present continuous changes to past continuous).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

During the Mughal era, several new market towns were being emerged along the trade routes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. emerged.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Emerge" is an intransitive verb, which has no object, so it cannot be used in the passive. The action also belongs to a definite past period ("During the Mughal era"), so the simple past is needed. So "were being emerged" must be "emerged".

◦ Corrected sentence: During the Mughal era, several new market towns emerged along the trade routes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "had been emerged" — this is again a passive of the intransitive verb "emerge", and the past perfect has no later past action to refer to.

 

• Option 3: "have emerged" — this is a present perfect, and it cannot be used with the definite past period "During the Mughal era".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "were being emerged" is a passive form of an intransitive verb.

 

NOTE

 

• intransitive verbs take no passive: The sun rose, The boy fell, Towns emerged, and not was rose, was fallen, were emerged.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

When the principal entered the hall, the students stand up and greeted her respectfully.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. stood up.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Actions that happen one after another in the past take the simple past. "Entered" and "greeted" are in the simple past, so "stand up" must be "stood up".

◦ Corrected sentence: When the principal entered the hall, the students stood up and greeted her respectfully.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "standing up" — this is a participle without an auxiliary, and it cannot act as the finite verb joined by "and" to "greeted".

 

• Option 3: "have stood up" — this is a present perfect, and it does not go with the past verbs "entered" and "greeted".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the present form "stand up" does not match the past verbs in the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• The bell rang and the students ran out (simple past for actions in sequence).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

While the security guard patrols the corridor, the lights suddenly went off.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. was patrolling.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The past continuous ("was / were + verb-ing") is used for a longer action in progress in the past that is interrupted by a shorter action in the simple past. "While" also takes the continuous form. So "patrols" must be "was patrolling".

◦ Corrected sentence: While the security guard was patrolling the corridor, the lights suddenly went off.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "had patrolled" — this is a past perfect, which shows a completed action, but "while" needs an action in progress.

 

• Option 2: "has patrolled" — this is a present perfect, and it does not suit the past clause "went off".

 

• Option 3: "is patrolling" — this is a present continuous, and it does not match the past verb "went off".

 

NOTE

 

• While I was walking, it began to rain; He was sleeping when the phone rang (past continuous interrupted by the simple past).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

It is high time the government takes strict action against illegal encroachments.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. took.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "It is (high) time + subject", the simple past is used to show that the action should have been done already. So "takes" must be "took".

◦ Corrected sentence: It is high time the government took strict action against illegal encroachments.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "will take" — a future form is not used after "It is high time".

 

• Option 2: "has taken" — a present perfect is not used after "It is high time", which needs the simple past.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the present form "takes" is not used after "It is high time".

 

NOTE

 

• It is time we left, It is high time you started (simple past after "It is (high) time").

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Over the last decade, the number of internet users in rural India increased dramatically.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. has increased.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Over the last decade" (a period that continues up to now) takes the present perfect, because the change is linked to the present. So "increased" must be "has increased", and it agrees with the singular "the number".

◦ Corrected sentence: Over the last decade, the number of internet users in rural India has increased dramatically.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "increases" — this is a simple present, which shows a habit or a general fact, and it does not suit "Over the last decade".

 

• Option 3: "had increased" — this is a past perfect, and it needs a past reference point, which the sentence does not have.

 

• Option 4: "will increase" — this is a future form, and it does not suit a period that has already passed.

 

NOTE

 

• Over the last few years, prices have risen; In recent years, the number of cars has grown (present perfect for a period up to now).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

When the inspector arrived, the workers have been fixing the last section of the pipeline.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. had been fixing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The past perfect continuous ("had been + verb-ing") is used for an action that was going on up to a point in the past when another past action happened. "Arrived" is the later past action, so "have been fixing" must be "had been fixing".

◦ Corrected sentence: When the inspector arrived, the workers had been fixing the last section of the pipeline.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "will be fixing" — this is a future continuous, and it does not suit the past verb "arrived".

 

• Option 2: "fix" — this is a simple present, and it does not suit the past verb "arrived".

 

• Option 3: "has been fixing" — this is a singular present perfect continuous, which neither agrees with "workers" nor suits the past clause.

 

NOTE

 

• When I reached, they had been waiting for an hour (past perfect continuous for an action going on up to a past point).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The company had relocated its headquarters to Pune in 2019 after signing a new lease.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. relocated.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "In 2019" is a definite past time, and a single completed past action takes the simple past. The past perfect needs a second, later past action, which the sentence does not have. So "had relocated" must be "relocated".

◦ Corrected sentence: The company relocated its headquarters to Pune in 2019 after signing a new lease.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "has relocated" — this is a present perfect, and it cannot be used with the definite past time "in 2019".

 

• Option 3: "was relocating" — this is a past continuous, which shows an action in progress, but the sentence states a completed event.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the past perfect "had relocated" has no later past action to refer to.

 

NOTE

 

• The company was founded in 1995, She joined the firm in 2019 (simple past with a definite past time).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The sprinkler starts working as soon as the soil will become dry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. becomes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a time clause introduced by as soon as, when, until, before or after, "will" is not used, and the simple present is used instead. So "will become" must be "becomes".

◦ Corrected sentence: The sprinkler starts working as soon as the soil becomes dry.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "would become" — "would" is not used in a present-time clause introduced by "as soon as".

 

• Option 2: "is becoming" — this is a present continuous, which shows a change in progress, while "as soon as" needs the simple present for a completed change.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "will" is not used in a time clause.

 

NOTE

 

• as soon as he arrives, when the water boils, until it stops (simple present in a time clause), and not as soon as he will arrive.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The new tax rules had not yet been notified by the ministry, so businesses are confused.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. have not yet been notified.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Yet" with a present result ("businesses are confused") takes the present perfect. The passive plural form is "have not been + past participle". So "had not yet been notified" must be "have not yet been notified".

◦ Corrected sentence: The new tax rules have not yet been notified by the ministry, so businesses are confused.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "was not yet notified" — this is a singular verb, which does not agree with "rules", and a simple past does not suit "yet" with a present result.

 

• Option 3: "has not yet notified" — this is a singular active verb, which does not agree with "rules", and the rules cannot notify anything.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the past perfect "had … been" needs a past reference point, while the result is in the present.

 

NOTE

 

• The results have not yet been declared, The train has not yet arrived (present perfect with "yet").

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

It is reported that the company has earned a record profit in the last quarter of 2019.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. earned.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "In the last quarter of 2019" is a definite past period, so the simple past is used and not the present perfect. So "has earned" must be "earned".

◦ Corrected sentence: It is reported that the company earned a record profit in the last quarter of 2019.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "is earning" — this is a present continuous, and it does not suit a definite past period.

 

• Option 2: "had earned" — this is a past perfect, and it needs a second, later past action, which the sentence does not have.

 

• Option 3: "earns" — this is a simple present, which shows a habit, and it does not suit "in the last quarter of 2019".

 

NOTE

 

• The company earned a profit in 2019, The film was released in March (simple past with a definite past time), and not has earned in 2019.
